directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Burmese is a vigorous heirloom okra producing long, tender, ribbed green pods on tall, productive plants that continue bearing heavily through the hottest part of summer, a season when many other vegetables slow down. It has a reputation among heirloom seed savers for strong yields and reliable performance across a range of Southern growing conditions. Harvest pods every day or two once production begins, picking at three to four inches for the most tender texture, since pods left too long on the plant quickly become tough and fibrous.

common_name: Silver Queen Okra (Pale Ivory-Green Ornamental Okra)

planting.note: Direct sow an inch deep after last frost when soil is above 65 degrees F; soak seeds overnight in warm water before planting to improve germination.

directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Silver Queen is an heirloom okra valued for its pale, silvery ivory-green pods and foliage, a striking, almost ghostly color that sets it apart from the deep green of most okra varieties and makes it as much an ornamental curiosity as a productive vegetable. The tender pods have the classic okra flavor and texture, well suited to frying, gumbo, and pickling, and the plant produces reliably through the heat of a Gulf South summer. Harvest young, at three to four inches, for the best tenderness, and pick regularly to keep the plant producing over a long season.

common_name: Baby Bubba Okra (AAS-Winning Dwarf Compact Okra)

planting.note: Direct sow an inch deep after last frost when soil is above 65 degrees F; soak seeds overnight in warm water before planting to improve germination.

directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Baby Bubba is a compact, dwarf okra cultivar bred specifically for smaller gardens and container growing, staying considerably shorter than standard okra varieties while still producing a good crop of tender, dark green, ribbed pods over a long summer season. Its shorter stature also makes harvesting easier, without needing a ladder or long reach for pods higher up on a tall plant. As with all okra, pick pods young, at two to four inches, and harvest every day or two during peak production to keep the compact plant setting new pods rather than diverting energy into maturing tough, oversized ones.
